test_contract:
Four independent contracts, one per item.

A1 — the observable contract: a status-line preset that lists `usage` renders the quota segment at 200 columns (all five windows plus tier) and STILL renders it at 80 columns; a preset whose ctx.usage is null renders byte-identical output to the pre-change build; and every preset outside the P1-chosen subset renders byte-identical to pre-change. A consumer who regresses this sees a quota indicator silently vanish at narrow widths, or — worse — see every existing user's `default` row change shape on upgrade. This is the one item in the wave where a mistake is visible to every user on day one.

A8 — the observable contract: under tmux with a ctrl+b prefix binding, the rendered footer hint reads `ctrl+b ctrl+b` while the key handed back to the input layer is still a single `ctrl+b`; outside tmux, with a non-prefix binding, and when the probe fails, the hint is the bare key and nothing throws. A regression is a footer that lies to the user about what to press.

A6 — the observable contract: a marked non-read tool called twice with a different tool interleaved is counted as TWO by the group header on the LIVE path AND the transcript rebuilt from history produces byte-identical output. The rebuild half is the load-bearing half: a missed membership site produces a transcript that folds differently live than on reload, which is a silent failure — no compile error, no test signal, only visible when a user reopens an old session. The negative half: an unmarked tool still renders standalone.

A5 — the observable contract: a synchronous block longer than the threshold driven from inside a NAMED phase makes the loader row show a stall indicator naming that phase, and a normal frame afterwards clears it. Separately, the per-phase frame-time values SUM to the existing total within tolerance — a decomposition, not a second clock. A regression is either a stall that is invisible when it matters, or an indicator that never goes away.

test_contract:
Two files, one idea: the status-line segment surface is a CLOSED set, and the two new tests defend that closure at the three places a contributor would actually break it.

`packages/tui/test/status-line-segment-closure.test.ts` defends the union<->registry agreement. The two catalogs are maintained by hand in two files (schema.ts:2-30 and segments.ts:919) and until now nothing checked the seam between them; the only coupling is a `Record<StatusLineSegmentId, ...>` annotation that catches union-widening at compile time but nothing catches registry drift. The consumer-visible failure if it regresses: someone adds a segment id, the build stays green, and the segment SILENTLY DISAPPEARS from the status line — `renderSegment` returns `{ content: "", visible: false }` at segments.ts:950-953, and component.ts:2590 / :2603 drops it via `if (rendered.visible && rendered.content)` with no warning, no log, nothing. A user sees a status line that is quietly missing a field they configured. The third test pins ALL_SEGMENT_IDS against the union, closing the `as StatusLineSegmentId[]` cast at segments.ts:957 that currently makes the reverse direction unchecked and that flows into the gallery inventory at cli/gallery-fixtures/segments.ts:19.

`packages/coding-agent/test/status-line-segment-picker.test.ts` defends the third catalog, the one the plan never mentions: settings.ts:280 and :287 register the pickers with `items: { values: STATUS_LINE_SEGMENT_IDS }`, so the interactive settings UI can only ever present ids from the frozen union. The consumer-visible failure if it regresses: a segment that renders fine in the gallery can never be selected in the actual settings UI, and a maintainer adding one discovers this only by trying it manually. The default assertion catches the paired drift — the config default and the picker's vocabulary disagreeing means `statusLine.leftSegments` defaults to something the picker cannot show.

Deliberately NOT tested, and why: the 'exactly one non-test setFrameProvider call site' invariant, the 'the barrel has no register*' invariant, and the 'the union has 27 members' count are all real findings but each is the banned source-grep / baked-constant shape under AGENTS.md — they read an implementation file or a constant and assert on its text, they break on a harmless refactor, and they pass while behavior is broken. They belong in the doc as prose. Likewise the current contents of CUSTOM_STATUS_LINE_DEFAULTS are NOT asserted: Sóng 1's A1 may legitimately change them, and pinning today's default is a landmine for the work that follows.

test_contract:
Four contracts, one per test file, none redundant.

(1) `packages/tui/test/wheel-acceleration.test.ts` defends THE MODEL: given a synthesized notch stream and the thresholds recorded in the measurement table, the returned row count is exactly the specified one. Detented wheel -> three notches for one physical detent stay at 1 row each, never 3. Continuous at ~20 ms -> climbs to the cap; at 500 ms -> stays at 1. Flip-then-flip-back inside the measured bounce window -> wheel mode on; no event for the measured idle-reset window -> off. A stream with no flip never enables wheel mode. Notches closer than the measured batch window count once. `ui.mouseWheelSpeedMultiplier = 0.5` multiplies the accelerated delta exactly ONCE (a double application is invisible in the model test but doubles the speed for the user). If this regresses, the user feels a wrong scroll speed on their own hardware and there is no way for them to tell you — only the threshold table can.

(2) `packages/tui/test/mouse.test.ts` defends THE WIRING: `routeSelectListMouse` hands `event.now` to `handleWheel` as a second argument, and `parseSgrMouse` stamps a `now` derived from the injected clock rather than calling `Date.now()` internally (so the test can assert the exact value). The two pre-existing assertions — the `toEqual` at :22-32 and the `baseEvent` literal at :126-134 — are the canary: if a future change drops the field from one construction path, they go red.

(3) `packages/coding-agent/test/notice-queue.test.ts` defends TWO contracts and the second one is the one that matters. First: supersession and folding — a keyed low-priority notice followed by an `immediate` notice whose `invalidates` names its key removes the first from the display permanently; the same key posted three times with `fold` accumulates into exactly one row; a notice arriving while another is showing queues rather than overwrites. Second, and NON-NEGOTIABLE: THE RENDER-LOCATION CONTRACT — a keyed notice appears in the notice container's children and is ABSENT from `chatContainer.children`; an unkeyed notice is still in `chatContainer.children` exactly as before. Without that assertion the build stays green while someone renders both branches into the transcript, which is precisely the unrequested behavior change the plan forbids. Plus one integration test driving a real compaction through `EventController` and asserting exactly ONE transient notice results, and a validation test proving 0 and negatives are rejected rather than applied.

(4) `packages/tui/test/transcript-viewer-scroll-chrome.test.ts` defends THE MARKER: scroll up, append a message, the divider shows with the right unread count, activating it returns to the bottom; change terminal width through at least three widths WHILE scrolled and the marker still points at the same message; and the plain transcript renders byte-identically with the chrome in place. The width test is the whole reason this item exists — a chrome header whose height varies shifts the viewport on every reflow even when the offset is unchanged. If this regresses, the divider drifts onto the wrong message the first time the user resizes their window mid-scroll, and nothing else catches it.

With `enabled` absent and with `enabled: false`, no process is ever created and the rendered status row is byte-identical to a baseline captured with the plugin never loaded. A consumer who installs this plugin and never touches the setting sees zero behavior change; if that regresses, a user's shell command starts running on every message in every session. The enabled-path cases defend the complementary contracts: each documented trigger produces exactly one visible update; a non-zero exit still updates; a hanging command still lets the row render (the silent-failure contract — without it a bad command manifests only as a status bar that quietly stops updating, and the non-exiting case is what proves the render path is not blocking on a child); rapid bursts coalesce to a single call; and 10,000-character plus tab-bearing output renders sanitized and within the row's width. D2 defends: the new segment reports the same hit rate as `cache_hit` for identical usage input, proving no second calculation can drift; the row contains no countdown and no TTL label (the entire point of the item — the reference implementation's countdown is a fake TTL that resets on every fresh API response, so porting it would ship a confidently wrong number under a color scale that reads as 'cache about to expire'); with no usage data the segment contributes nothing rather than guessing; and the segment reads no wall-clock constant, which is the regression guard against the countdown being reintroduced. What a consumer sees if either regresses: for C2, shell commands the user never authorized running; for D2, a cache-health number that is confidently wrong in exactly the situation a user is watching it for.

gate:
Three gates, all able to fail.

G1 (can fail): `bun run check:ts` exits non-zero if the DALTONIZE_TARGET_HUE indexing of `resolvedColors` does not typecheck, or if the new module violates the no-`any` / top-level-import rules. It was green at baseline, so a red is attributable to this change.

G2 (can fail): the contrast-4.5 harness goes red if any of the 101 builtin themes has a remapped token that fails its paired-background ratio. This gate is expected to be the expensive one -- it will likely surface themes that were already marginal before this change, and those become the remediation list rather than a reason to lower the threshold silently.

G3 (can fail, and is the one that matters): the negative-identity test goes red if the colorBlindMode branch is moved above `resolveThemeColors` (which would apply the remap to unresolved `$var` strings and change every theme regardless of the flag), if the branch is widened to a path that runs when the flag is false, or if the remap mutates shared state that leaks into the flag-off theme. All three are easy mistakes and all three are invisible in review.

A gate that cannot fail would be 'the file exists' or '99 palettes were iterated' -- neither proves the remap happened or that the flag still gates it.

test_contract:
Three contracts, each with a named observable failure.

(1) POSITIVE COVERAGE. With colorBlindMode on, all five tokens in DALTONIZE_TARGET_HUE differ from their colorBlindMode-off values. Consumer-visible failure: a red-green colorblind user enables Color-Blind Mode, the success tick and the clean-git indicator stay green, and they read a successful tool call as an added diff line -- the exact misread this setting is supposed to prevent. Assert by building a Theme from a known palette both ways and comparing the five token values, not by asserting the literal output hex (the hues are a human decision, per open_questions, so pinning them would make every future tweak a test edit).

(2) EVERY OUTPUT IS A VALID HEX. After createTheme with colorBlindMode on, each of the five tokens matches /^#[0-9a-f]{6}$/i, for all 101 builtin themes. Consumer-visible failure: a theme throws inside Bun.color at render time, or the TUI emits a broken SGR sequence and the diff view corrupts. This is the check that would have caught a number or empty-string value sneaking through the remap -- today guarded only by startsWith("#").

(3) NEGATIVE IDENTITY -- the strongest and cheapest. With colorBlindMode omitted or false, every token of every builtin theme is byte-identical to the value before this change. Consumer-visible failure: a user who never enabled Color-Blind Mode gets a silently different UI after an upgrade. This is the contract that makes the change safe to ship, and it is what pins the branch to 'only when the flag is set'.

(4) CONTRAST, across all 101 builtin themes, for the five pairs listed in step 7. Consumer-visible failure: after enabling the mode, the dirty-git indicator becomes unreadable against the status-line background in some theme. This is the only test that generalizes past the five tokens -- it is the regression net the 101-palette sweep exists to provide.

Per AGENTS.md: no `mock.module()`, no `mock.*` at all, no source-grep of any .ts file, no `expect(true).toBe(true)`, no bare `not.toThrow()`, no non-empty-string assertions. If the two files get folded into one, keep these four assertions distinct -- they defend different regressions.
